Bishr makes no distinction here between effects in which the actor’s will directly plays a part and effects that follow without any further act of will.
So where does the difference between Abū al-Hudhayl and Bishr come from?
Al-Ashʿarī reports that Abū al-Hudhayl believed God could keep a heavy stone suspended in the air for a long time without allowing it to fall, and that the stone could remain still.
He also believed that fire and cotton could come together without the cotton burning.
Al-Ashʿarī therefore says that al-ʿAllāf “disagreed with the people of rational inquiry on this question.”

If we take this report about al-ʿAllāf at face value, the difference between his theory of generated action and Bishr’s would seem to come from Abū al-Hudhayl’s tendency to deny the principle of causality in nature and to deny the law of motion.
But denying causality would contradict one of the two principles on which the Muʿtazilite idea of generated action—and the responsibility connected with it—was built.
One of those principles was causality.
The other was human freedom of choice.
We will see, however, that there is a mistake in understanding al-ʿAllāf’s position in this way.
Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, by contrast, clearly bases his view on the principle of causality.
In this respect, his position fits directly with the wider Muʿtazilite idea.
We find the same consistency in another leading Muʿtazilite thinker, al-Khayyāṭ.
Al-Khayyāṭ connects generated action directly to both the necessary causal order of nature and the law of motion.
He explains his position with two examples.
In the first, a person sends a stone rolling from the top of a mountain. The stone falls toward the ground. Suppose the person dies before the stone reaches the bottom.
The stone’s continued fall after the person’s death is still generated by the act of releasing it.
Its movement must therefore still be attributed to the person who set it in motion, and to no one else.
In the second example, a man shoots an arrow at a target and dies after the arrow has left the bow but before it reaches the target.
The arrow’s continued movement after the archer’s death is generated by his shot.
It therefore remains attributable to him and to no one else.
In both examples, an act begun by a person continues to produce effects after that person has died.
This gives the question two sides.
One concerns purely natural causality and, as we will see, the law of motion.
The other concerns legal and moral responsibility.
For the Muʿtazilites, however, the two cannot really be separated.

If a generated act remains attributable to the person who began the original action even after that person has died, this is because that person remains the first cause of everything that follows from the original act.
This is why Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf could say, quite literally rather than figuratively, that the dead can kill the living, healthy, and strong.
The Muʿtazilites base their judgment here on two principles.
The first is that events follow fixed laws of nature—in this case, the law of causality.
The second is that human beings are responsible for their own actions because they freely choose them.
That responsibility applies not only to acts they perform directly, but also to acts and effects generated by those direct acts.
And it is precisely the principle of causality that allows responsibility to extend from the first act to everything that follows from it.

There are also signs in some Muʿtazilite texts that they took the law of motion into account in this question. We see this especially in al-Khayyāṭ’s philosophical explanation of why the movement of an arrow should be attributed to the person who shot it.

Al-Khayyāṭ says that when someone shoots an arrow, its movement must be one of four things: an act of God, an act of the arrow itself, an act with no agent behind it, or an act of the person who shot it. He then argues against the first three possibilities and accepts only the fourth.
We can clearly see that his whole argument rests on the principle of necessary causation in nature, alongside the established Muʿtazilite principle that human beings freely choose their actions.

Al-Khayyāṭ rejects the idea that God causes the arrow to move on the following grounds. Human beings have the power to act and freely choose their actions. God does not enter into human actions or force people to perform them. If God were the one who caused the arrow to move, then a person could shoot an arrow and God could simply choose not to make it move. The arrow would then remain where it was. For al-Khayyāṭ, this is impossible.
We can see why he considers it impossible. An arrow failing to move after being shot would violate the law of motion, which necessarily requires it to move once it has been launched.

Al-Khayyāṭ says that if we accepted this impossibility, we would also have to accept many others. If God could choose not to make an arrow move after it had been shot, then we would also have to allow, for example, that an extremely strong person could press a sword against the back of someone’s neck, yet God might not cause the sword to cut it. Or fire could be brought into contact with esparto grass, yet God might not cause it to burn.

In other words, al-Khayyāṭ considers it impossible for a neck not to be cut when a sword is pressed against it with great force, or for esparto grass not to burn when it comes into contact with fire. And it is clear that these things are impossible for him because they would violate fixed laws of nature—above all the law of causation, together here with the law of motion.

Al-Khayyāṭ also rejects the second possibility: that the movement of the arrow is an act performed by the arrow itself. His reason is that an arrow is an inanimate object. It is neither alive nor capable of acting. It cannot perform an action because it has no choice, will, or knowledge.
This follows the Muʿtazilite understanding of human action, according to which an agent must possess all three: choice, will, and knowledge.

As for the third possibility—that the arrow’s movement is an act with no agent behind it—al-Khayyāṭ rejects this by saying that, if such a thing were possible, a book could exist without anyone having written it. That, he says, is impossible.
Why is it impossible? Surely the point is that a natural event cannot occur without a cause.
From everything we have seen so far, it appears that the Muʿtazilites came close to recognizing that nature has objective laws of its own and that natural events take place according to those laws.
We do not find a direct statement from them explicitly setting out this idea. But we do find statements on other subjects that come very close to expressing it.

We can return, for example, to our earlier discussion of the “indivisible part,” and to the different Muʿtazilite views on substance and accident. There we find attempts to understand the laws of nature in whatever way the knowledge available in their own time allowed.

Consider, too, a statement by al-Naẓẓām reported by al-Baghdādī. Al-Naẓẓām says that one kind of thing cannot produce two opposite kinds of action, just as fire cannot both heat and cool. In other words, each kind of body produces a particular kind of effect.

Al-Shahrastānī reports another statement by al-Naẓẓām that gives an example of how every natural body is subject to fixed laws. If a stone is pushed, it moves. Once the force of the push has run its course, the stone naturally returns to its place—that is, it does so because of its own nature.
Taken together, these two statements show al-Naẓẓām making a serious attempt to recognize that the laws of nature exist objectively.
We find similar attempts among other thinkers as well.

Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī, for example, argues that whatever occurs in bodies—motion and rest, color and taste, smell, heat and cold, moisture and dryness—is produced by the body itself according to its nature.

He expresses the same idea in another way when he says that an inanimate body produces the accidents that occur in it according to its own nature. Life is the action of what is alive; power is the action of what has power; and death is the action of what is dead.

Elsewhere Muʿammar states the idea even more explicitly. He says that the movements of the heavenly bodies, along with everything in the world that moves or remains still, joins or separates, touches or moves apart, are the acts of something other than God.
In other words, whatever happens to the heavenly bodies results from natural laws present within those bodies themselves. It does not come to them from an outside divine action.
We find similar language in al-Jāḥiẓ, who was himself a Muʿtazilite. He says, for example, that bodies have their own natures and actions specific to them.

At first sight, a statement attributed to Abū al-Hudhayl, al-Iskāfī, and al-Jubbāʾī might seem to deny the existence of such objective laws in nature. But this impression comes from misunderstanding what they mean.

Al-Ashʿarī reports that these three thinkers said it was possible for a heavy stone to remain together with the air for some time without God creating its descent or fall, so that it remained still. They also said that fire and cotton could be brought together without burning taking place.
Does this mean that they denied the natural law that makes a heavy stone fall through the air, or the law that makes combustible material such as cotton burn when it comes into contact with fire?
Their point is that these natural laws do not necessarily produce their effects immediately. Another natural factor may temporarily prevent the expected result.

This is how we understand the phrase “for some time” in the passage reported by al-Ashʿarī. The statement does not say without qualification that a heavy stone can remain in the air without falling, or that fire can touch cotton without burning it. It places a limit on this possibility: it can happen only for a period of time.

And in scientific terms, such a situation can indeed last for a certain period. In the case of the stone, this is the interval between its upward movement and its fall. In the case of fire, it is the period during which some natural cause delays the fire’s effect.

So here we have examples from major Muʿtazilite thinkers that show very early attempts within Arab-Islamic thought to recognize objective laws of nature. These attempts came before the age of practical scientific discoveries, when the existence of such laws could be demonstrated directly through experiment.
These examples also reveal early expressions of materialism within Arab-Islamic metaphysical thought during its great flowering in the Muʿtazilite period.
We might even say that these expressions represent a particular historical form of materialism—one shaped by the conditions of medieval Arab-Islamic society.
F — Causality: Between Determinism and Freedom
We said earlier that, for the Muʿtazilites, there was no separation between necessary causation in nature and the responsibility that follows from causation in human social life.

We should also remember that, in their view, human responsibility rests on freedom of the will. Their refusal to separate objective necessity from human freedom therefore shows a striking rational insight. In an early and undeveloped form, it points toward an awareness of the dialectical relationship between “necessity and freedom.”
But we should not take this too far.

The Muʿtazilites made a basic and important distinction between causes in nature and causes in human society. Natural processes operate through mechanical necessity, while human actions include an additional element: the will.
This follows from one of the most basic principles of Muʿtazilite thought: human beings freely choose their actions.

They believed that human beings alone possess reason in the special sense that matters here. Reason gives us the ability to compare different possibilities, choose the one we think is best, will that choice, and then act on it. This is why the Muʿtazilites hold human beings responsible for their actions in both morality and metaphysics.
Because they distinguish so sharply between natural causes and human causes, they also understand the relationship between cause and effect differently depending on the kind of action involved.

When an action comes directly from a person’s will and freedom of choice, the connection between cause and effect is immediate. A voluntary act has only one direct cause: the first cause in which will is joined to the practical ability to act, which the Muʿtazilites call istiṭāʿa, or capacity.
But once other actions are generated by that first act, the relationship changes. The same is true of all involuntary actions, including the processes of nature.

In such cases, the connection between the first voluntary cause and the later involuntary effects remains in place, no matter how many intermediate causes and effects appear between them. The first cause, which began in the human will, continues to stand behind a series of later effects even though the intermediate causes themselves contain no element of will.
The example of the arrow makes this clearer.
Here we find both kinds of action. First there is the voluntary act: the action that comes directly from the will of the person shooting the arrow. This is the act of shooting.
Then there are the actions generated by that first act—for example, the arrow striking one target or another even though the archer did not intend to hit it.
The act of shooting itself is voluntary because it follows directly from a voluntary cause. What comes after it does not follow directly from the will and is therefore not voluntary.
Voluntary causation is limited to the act produced directly by the will. It does not extend in the same way to all the later events produced by that act.

Yet those later events do not lose their connection with the first cause—the original act of shooting. The connection simply changes in character. From that point on, the events follow the necessary principle of causation that governs nature, rather than the kind of causation that governs voluntary human action.

In short, a cause in nature can produce a whole chain of successive effects. Its connection with the final effect remains in place no matter how many other natural causes and effects come between them.
A voluntary human cause, by contrast, has only one direct effect: the act produced immediately by the will.
Once that act produces further effects, those effects belong to the other category. They become natural events governed by necessary causation rather than by the will.
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf expressed this Muʿtazilite position by saying that a person’s “acts of the heart cannot exist when capacity is absent. Capacity accompanies them at the moment of the act.”
By “acts of the heart,” he means voluntary acts.

His point, then, is that voluntary action can exist only where the person has the power to carry it out. And that power exists at the moment the action is performed—when the will is actually being put into effect.

Anything that happens after that original act and is generated by it has moved beyond the agent’s direct power, because it has moved beyond the agent’s will. From that point on, it is governed only by the natural laws of motion.
Abū al-Hudhayl calls these generated or involuntary actions “acts of the limbs,” as opposed to “acts of the heart.”

Al-Shahrastānī says that Abū al-Hudhayl allowed “acts of the limbs” to proceed from a human being even when direct capacity was no longer present—that is, even when the will was no longer controlling those acts. He also says that Abū al-Hudhayl regarded the capacity as coming before them.
What this means is that, for acts of the limbs, it is enough that will or capacity existed earlier, together with the first act that generated the later ones.

This is the basis on which the Muʿtazilites hold people responsible not only for their first voluntary act but also for the actions generated by it, as we saw earlier in our discussion of actions generated by human action.
Al-Iskāfī gives an even clearer distinction between voluntary and generated acts.

He describes a voluntary act as “every act that can take place only through intention, and whose every part requires renewed resolve, intention toward it, and will for it. Such an act lies outside the category of generation and within the category of direct action.”
A generated act, by contrast, is “every act that may occur by mistake, without intention toward it or will for it.”
On the same question, Muʿammar says that “the human being has no act except the will, whether directly or by generation.”
